title: Numbers and time
seoTitle: Turkish numbers, telling time, days and months
intro: Turkish numbers are regular: learn ten digits and a few round numbers, and you can build any number by putting the words in a row, *yirmi beş* (25), *iki bin yirmi altı* (2026). This unit also covers the singular noun after a number (*iki kitap*, two books), ordinals (*birinci*, first), the clock, dates, ages and prices. Several of them reuse the case endings you already know.

blocks.text: The numbers from zero to ten, then the tens, a hundred and a thousand. These twenty-two words are all you need.

**Building numbers.** Put the parts in a row, the biggest first, each as a separate word: *on bir* (11), *yirmi beş* (25), *yüz on* (110), *üç yüz kırk* (340). Hundreds and thousands multiply: *iki yüz* (200), *beş bin* (5,000), *on bin* (10,000).
**No bir before yüz and bin.** A hundred is just *yüz* and a thousand just *bin*, never *bir yüz* or *bir bin*. A million, though, is *bir milyon*.

**Suffixes on digits.** A suffix on a number written in digits takes an apostrophe, as in [unit 5](gp-apostrophe), and follows the sound of the last word you say: *3'te* (*üçte*, at three), *6'da* (*altıda*), *10'a* (*ona*), *1923'te* (*üçte*), *2026'da* (*altıda*).

items.en: This book is three hundred pages long.
There are twenty-two students in the class.

items.tr: İstanbul'da on beş milyon insan var.
items.en: There are fifteen million people in Istanbul.
I'm coming at three.

blocks.text: Turkish writes a dot between thousands and a comma for decimals, the other way round from English: *1.000* is a thousand, and *2,5* is two and a half, said *iki virgül beş*.
In shops and cafés you'll often hear *tane* (piece, item) after a number: *İki tane çay, lütfen* (Two teas, please). It adds nothing to the meaning; *İki çay, lütfen* is just as good.

sections.title: İki kitap: the singular after numbers

blocks.text: After a number, the noun stays singular: *iki kitap* (two books), *üç çocuk* (three children), *on beş gün* (fifteen days). The number already says there is more than one, so `-lAr` would say it twice. The same goes for *kaç* (how many), *birkaç* (a few) and *çok* (many, a lot of).

items.en: I have two brothers and sisters.
How many children do you have?
How many of you are there? There are four of us.
There are a lot of books here.
We're in Izmir for a few days.
Three students are coming.

blocks.text: The verb usually stays singular as well: *Üç öğrenci geliyor* (Three students are coming). You'll sometimes hear a plural verb with people, *Üç öğrenci geliyorlar*, but the singular is never wrong.
*İki kitaplar* and *çok insanlar* are wrong. The plural appears only when no number or quantity word is there: *Kitaplar masada* (The books are on the table).
Before a noun, *çok* means **many** or **a lot of**: *çok kitap*. Before an adjective it means **very**: *çok güzel*, as in [unit 1](a1-u01).

Add `-(I)ncI` to a number to make an ordinal (*sıra sayısı*): *birinci* (first), *ikinci* (second), *üçüncü* (third). After a vowel the first I drops: *ikinci*, *altıncı*, *yedinci*. The t of *dört* softens before the vowel: *dördüncü*. In a longer number only the last word takes the suffix: *yirmi birinci* (twenty-first).

*Kaçıncı?* asks which one in order: *Kaçıncı kattasın?* (Which floor are you on?) *Üçüncü kattayım.* (I'm on the third floor.) In digits, an ordinal is written with a full stop, *3. kat*, or with an apostrophe and the end of the suffix, *3'üncü kat*.

items.en: Our apartment is on the fourth floor.
The second door is the bathroom.
What grade are you in?
This is our tenth lesson.

blocks.text: *İlk* (first) and *son* (last) are everyday alternatives: *ilk gün* (the first day), *son ders* (the last lesson). *Birinci* is more usual for ranks, floors and numbered lists.

*Saat kaç?* (What time is it?) is answered with *saat* and a number: *Saat üç.* (It's three o'clock.) Half past is *buçuk*, after the hour: *Saat üç buçuk* (3:30). Half past twelve has a word of its own: *Saat yarım* (12:30).

For minutes past the hour, the hour takes the accusative and the verb is *geçiyor* (is passing): *Saat üçü on geçiyor* (It's ten past three). For minutes to the hour, the hour takes the dative, followed by *var* (there are): *Saat üçe on var* (It's ten to three; literally, there are ten to three). A quarter is *çeyrek*.

**At what time?** *Saat kaçta?* asks when something happens. Whole and half hours take the locative: *saat üçte* (at three), *üç buçukta* (at half past three). With minutes, *geçiyor* becomes *geçe* and *var* becomes *kala*: *üçü on geçe* (at ten past three), *üçe çeyrek kala* (at a quarter to three).

**The hours with case endings.** The usual rules apply: a buffer y after a vowel (*ikiyi*, *altıya*), t after a voiceless consonant (*üçte*), and the t of *dört* softens before a vowel (*dördü*, *dörde*, but *dörtte*).

items.en: The lesson starts at nine.
What time are you coming? At half past seven.
The train arrives at twenty past five.
It's five to two.
The film starts at a quarter past eight.

blocks.text: **The 24-hour clock.** Timetables, shops and the news use the 24-hour clock, written with a dot and read as plain numbers: *14.30* is *on dört otuz*, and *saat 14.30'da* means at 14:30.
In speech, *sabah* (morning) and *akşam* (evening) make the hour clear: *sabah yedide* (at seven in the morning), *akşam sekizde* (at eight in the evening).
Past the hour takes the accusative, to the hour the dative: *dördü çeyrek geçiyor* (4:15), *dörde çeyrek var* (3:45). And *Saat kaç?* asks the time now, *Saat kaçta?* the time of an event.

sections.title: Pazartesi, ekim: days, months and dates

blocks.text: The week starts on Monday:
The months:

**Capital letters.** Day and month names are common nouns, written in lowercase: *pazartesi*, *ekimde* (in October). In a specific date they take a capital, and a suffix after them takes an apostrophe: *29 Ekim 1923*, *15 Ekim Perşembe*, *23 Nisan'da* (on 23 April).

**Saying a date.** Day, month, year, with ordinary numbers: *29 Ekim 1923* is read *yirmi dokuz ekim bin dokuz yüz yirmi üç*. To ask the date, say *Bugün ayın kaçı?*, literally the how-many of the month. The answer is *Ayın on beşi* (the fifteenth) or *Bugün 15 Ekim*. To ask the day: *Bugün günlerden ne?* (What day is it today?) *Bugün perşembe.*

**When?** A day needs no ending, *Cumartesi geliyorum* (I'm coming on Saturday), or is followed by *günü*: *salı günü* (on Tuesday). Months and years take the locative: *ekimde* (in October), *2026'da* (in 2026), *23 Nisan'da* (on 23 April).

items.en: What day is it today? It's Friday.
What's the date today?
Schools are closed on 29 October.
We're going to Istanbul in May.
What are you doing on Saturday?

blocks.text: **Seasons.** *İlkbahar* or *bahar* (spring), *yaz* (summer), *sonbahar* (autumn, fall), *kış* (winter). Spring and autumn take the locative, *ilkbaharda*, *sonbaharda*; summer and winter have fixed forms, *yazın* (in summer) and *kışın* (in winter).
*Pazartesi* is *pazar ertesi*, the day after Sunday, and *cumartesi* is *cuma ertesi*, the day after Friday. *Pazar* also means **market**.
Don't capitalize a day or a month on its own: *ekimde*, *pazartesi günü*, not *Ekimde* or *Pazartesi günü*, unless it starts a sentence. The capital and the apostrophe belong to dates: *29 Ekim'de*.

sections.title: Kaç yaşındasın? Kaç lira? Ages and prices

blocks.text: To ask someone's age: *Kaç yaşındasın?* (How old are you?), or politely *Kaç yaşındasınız?* The answer puts the number before *yaşında* and adds the endings of **to be**: *Yirmi beş yaşındayım* (I'm twenty-five).
*Yaşında* is *yaş* (age) + `-(s)I` + n + `-DA`, built like *evinde* in [unit 10](gp-pronominal-n): literally **in its year**. It stays the same for every person; only the ending of **to be** changes.

items.en: My daughter is five.
My grandfather is eighty.
How old are you?

blocks.text: **Prices.** *Kaç lira?* or *Ne kadar?* (How much is it?) The Turkish lira (*lira*, written TL or ₺) has a hundred *kuruş*: *on beş lira* (15 TL), *yirmi lira elli kuruş* (20.50 TL). To ask the price per kilo, Turkish uses the genitive of [unit 10](gp-genitive-possessive): *Elmanın kilosu kaç lira?*, literally the apple's kilo.

items.en: How much is this jacket?
A simit is twenty lira.
How much is a kilo of apples?
Two coffees: a hundred and fifty lira.

blocks.text: Age isn't something you **have** or **are** in Turkish, but something you are **in**: *Yirmi yaşındayım*, not *Yirmi yaşım var* or *Yirmi yaşıyım*.

summary: Numbers are built word by word, the biggest first: *yirmi beş, yüz on, bin dokuz yüz yirmi üç*. No *bir* before *yüz* and *bin*.
After a number, *kaç*, *birkaç* or *çok*, the noun stays singular: *iki kitap, kaç kişi, birkaç gün, çok insan*.
Ordinals add `-(I)ncI`: *birinci, ikinci, üçüncü, dördüncü*. *Kaçıncı?* asks which one.
*Saat kaç?* *Üçü çeyrek geçiyor* (3:15), *üçe çeyrek var* (2:45). *Saat kaçta?* *Üçte, üç buçukta, üçü çeyrek geçe, üçe çeyrek kala*.
Days and months are lowercase except in a date: *pazartesi, ekimde*, but *29 Ekim 1923*, *23 Nisan'da*.
Age: *Kaç yaşındasın? Yirmi yaşındayım.* Prices: *Kaç lira? Ne kadar?*
